title: Ang 1352: Jaijavanti
hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur's four hymns in the last raga
tomorrow: after the last raga, verses in a style older than the Gurus. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page of Prabhati: Namdev turning inward, and Beni's man with a knife under the marks. The last bhagats. Now, one short raga is left.

A song stuck in your head came with a tune you didn't pick. Change the tune and the same words land differently. Jaijavanti is the last raga in the Granth, and on ang 1352 it holds four hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru. That answers yesterday's question. It also opens an argument Sikh musicians still have: should these words be sung in the raga the Guru named, or in a tune anyone can sing?
screen: `SAME WORDS, NEW TUNE.` → `THE NINTH GURU'S FOUR HYMNS.` → `THE RAGA, OR A TUNE FOR ALL?`

segments.voice: First, the hymns. They're short and urgent. In paraphrase, one says: remember the Lord, remember; that's your real work. Another asks the mind: what will become of you? A third sounds like a clock: it's passing, it's passing, this life is slipping by. The fourth says: take shelter in the Name. Now the two views, each at its best. Some ragis and kirtan teachers hold to the raga. Every hymn in the Granth carries a raga in its heading, and they hear that heading as part of the hymn. Jaijavanti's mood was chosen for these words; sing them in another tune and something the Guru gave goes missing. Their case: the heading is in the Guru's book, so it isn't decoration. Other Sikhs sing Gurbani in simpler tunes a whole hall can join. Their case: the Gurus sang among ordinary people, and a hymn everyone can sing reaches hearts a trained-only raga might miss. Both sides love the same words. One points to the heading; the other points to the sangat singing together. Nobody has to win today. Listen for what each side protects. One guards the Guru's chosen mood. The other guards the room's voice.
screen: `FOUR SHORT, URGENT HYMNS.` · `ONE VIEW: THE HEADING IS THE GURU'S.` · `OTHER VIEW: A TUNE THE ROOM CAN SING.` · `EACH SIDE PROTECTS SOMETHING.` · then, large: `THE LAST RAGA.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound near you that rises and falls: a fan, traffic, the fridge, your own breath. Follow it through the sit without naming it, the way a raga's mood moves under the words. If you'd like, read all four hymns on ang 1352 first.
Ang 1352. Jaijavanti, the last raga, with four hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur and an old argument about how to sing them.
To keep: the last raga, short hymns about a life slipping by, and two loving ways to sing them. See you tomorrow.
